title: Group chat and presence
like: team chat like Slack or Discord
brief: Teams talk in channels with many people. Everyone sees messages in the same order, sees who is online and who is typing, and gets notified when mentioned. At nine every morning thousands of workplaces start at once, and one announcement can reach a channel of tens of thousands.

clarify.q: Must everyone see messages in the same order?
clarify.a: Yes. A conversation that reads differently for two people is broken.
No. It is a guess that expires in half a minute. It is gone if nobody refreshes it.

clarify.q: How big is the biggest channel?
clarify.a: A company-wide channel might have 50,000 members. A message there reaches everyone online.
A record of who did what, and proof that their messages are encrypted with keys managed in a key service.

notes: Presence updates ("online", "typing") are the biggest source of events (approx.).
A message sent in a 50,000-person channel becomes up to 50,000 deliveries.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Presence and typing events per second at peak
Deliveries from one message in the biggest channel

hints: Presence changes constantly and is worthless after a minute. Should it live in the same database as messages?
Keep presence in a cache with a short expiry and let it fade on its own. Messages need a store that keeps order. Pub/sub copies one message to every gateway that has a member of the channel.
Replay and live handoff must avoid gaps and duplicates without unlimited fanout. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Treat three kinds of data as three systems. Messages are durable and ordered: a store built for appends, one writer per channel. Presence is temporary: a cache with expiry. Delivery is a fanout: pub/sub copies each message once per gateway, and each gateway pushes to its own connections. The compliance asks are met by a key service and an audit log.

designs.name: Messages, presence and fanout kept apart
designs.why: The gateways hold the connections. Chat servers order and save each message, then publish it once. Pub/sub hands it to each gateway that needs it. Presence lives in a cache and fades by itself. A key service and audit log cover the compliance checks.

tradeoffs: One writer per channel keeps order simple, but a very busy channel is then limited by that writer. Splitting a channel breaks the order guarantee.
Presence in a cache with an expiry is cheap and self-cleaning, but it can be wrong for up to half a minute after a phone vanishes.
Delivering a message to 50,000 people costs 50,000 pushes. Sending it to a gateway once and letting the gateway fan out keeps the central servers calm.
A partition forces a choice: keep chatting on both sides and fix the order afterwards, or pause one side. Chat usually keeps sending and merges later.
Encryption and audit logs add a small cost and a lookup per message, and they are what a business customer asks for first.
editorial.realWorld: Team chat apps hold millions of connections open at the same time (approx.), with presence kept in memory and messages kept in sharded stores. A company-wide message can reach tens of thousands of people in about a second.

correctness.prompt: Group chat and presence: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Agree on channel message order while treating presence as expiring soft state. Everyone must recover the same committed channel sequence. Presence tolerates loss and should not be a permanent truth record. Replay and live handoff must avoid gaps and duplicates without unlimited fanout.

fields.label: Step 1. Two channel writers race. What orders their messages?
options: Each socket server chooses its own order
One fenced sequencer per channel with durable message ids
fields.explanation: Everyone must recover the same committed channel sequence.

fields.label: Step 2. A socket server dies without sending offline updates. What happens to presence?
options: Users remain online until a durable logout arrives
fields.explanation: Presence tolerates loss and should not be a permanent truth record.

fields.label: Step 3. A large channel reconnects together. What recovers missed messages?
options: Broadcast the entire history over every new socket
Bounded replay from durable per-channel cursors, then live subscription
fields.explanation: Replay and live handoff must avoid gaps and duplicates without unlimited fanout.

correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 6250 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $45337. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
